short_title: Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel
full_title: HACIENDA SAN ISIDRO/SILOS FARMS AND REY SILOS LLAMADO, PETITIONERS, VS. LUCITO VILLARUEL AND HELEN VILLARUEL, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Labor Law and Social Legislation
syllabus_topic: III. Employment Relationship > C. Kinds of Employment > 5. Seasonal
topics: Second-paragraph proviso of Art. 295 applies only to casual employees
Freedom to work for other farms; Mercado distinguished
Pakyaw workers and the control test

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45)

doctrine:
**A seasonal employee becomes a regular employee when (1) the employee performs work or services that are seasonal in nature and (2) is employed to perform such work or services for more than one season.** The Court deduced these requisites from earlier cases and stated them "for the guidance of the bench and the bar." Under the first paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code, the seasonal exception covers only employment "for the duration of the season," i.e., one season. A seasonal employee rehired for more than one season falls back under the general rule of regular employment. **The basis of regular seasonal status is this first paragraph, not the proviso of the second paragraph** (at least one year of service, continuous or broken). That proviso applies only to casual employees, i.e., those not covered by the first paragraph (*Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.*; *Mercado*). The CA erred in treating the worker as a casual employee who became regular through the proviso.

Freedom to offer one's services to other farm owners does not negate regular status, as long as the worker is hired repeatedly for the same activities and not merely on and off for any single phase of agricultural work. *Mercado v. NLRC* was distinguished, as explained in *Hacienda Fatima*. Pakyaw is a method of paying wages, not the relationship itself. Pakyaw workers are regular employees if they are subject to the employer's control, and the control test requires only the existence of the right to control, not its actual exercise (reiterated from *Gapayao v. Fulo*).

**Caution:** In its Resolution of August 11, 2025, the Court granted the employer's motion for reconsideration, set aside this Decision, and reversed the CA. The Resolution kept the two requisites and the pakyaw rule. It held, however, that the worker failed to prove by substantial evidence that the employer had the right to control the manner and means of her work. It also rejected the inference that control exists simply because she worked on the employer's farm. See *Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution)*.
facts:
Spouses Lucito and Helen Villaruel worked in Hacienda San Isidro in Himamaylan, Negros Occidental. The hacienda was administered by Rey Silos Llamado and formed part of Silos Farms, owned by Fidel Silos. On December 18, 2009 and April 7, 2010, the spouses filed separate complaints against petitioners. They sought relief for illegal dismissal, underpayment of wages, service incentive leave pay, and attorney's fees, and the cases were consolidated.

On February 14, 2011, the Labor Arbiter found that Lucito was dismissed for just cause but without due process, and awarded him P5,000 nominal damages. The LA held that Helen was a regular employee who had been illegally dismissed, and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The NLRC first granted petitioners' partial appeal and held on September 30, 2011 that Helen was not an employee. On the spouses' MR, however, it reinstated the LA decision with modifications on January 27, 2012. It declared both dismissals illegal and awarded Helen P195,456.95.

Petitioners filed a petition for certiorari with the CA. On March 27, 2013, the CA held that Helen was not an employee because she failed to prove the element of control. On the spouses' MR, the CA issued an Amended Decision on January 9, 2015. It held that Helen was a regular employee who had been illegally dismissed, and awarded her backwages and separation pay. The CA reasoned that her sugar-farming work was necessary or desirable to petitioners' business. It added that, because she did not fit any category in the first paragraph of Art. 280, she was a casual employee under the second paragraph who became regular after at least one year of service. The CA denied petitioners' partial MR on July 20, 2015.

Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition on the sole issue of whether Helen, a seasonal worker in a sugar plantation, should be considered a regular employee. The Court denied the petition on November 9, 2015, but on petitioners' MR it reinstated the petition on November 7, 2016. Petitioners did not dispute that Helen did seasonal work in a yearly cycle. They argued as follows:
- She worked only sparingly, on a pakyaw basis.
- She was not required to report daily or keep definite hours, and she ran her own sari-sari store.
- They did not control how she worked.
- Under *Gapayao*, citing *Mercado*, seasonal workers who are free to contract their services with other farm owners are not regular employees.
issues: Whether Helen, an admittedly seasonal worker, is a regular employee, and whether the CA correctly based that status on the proviso of the second paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code.
Whether Helen's freedom to offer her services to other farm owners negates regular seasonal employment.
Whether Helen's engagement on a pakyaw basis, allegedly without petitioners' control, negates regular employment.
ruling:
**1. Yes, Helen is a regular seasonal employee, but the CA's reasoning was wrong.** The LA, the NLRC and the CA had uniformly found her a regular employee. The Court said that factual findings of expert quasi-judicial agencies, when affirmed by the CA, are accorded respect and even finality, and it did not disturb this finding. It nevertheless corrected the CA's reasoning "for the guidance of the bench and the bar." A proviso qualifies only the clause immediately preceding it. The second paragraph of Art. 295 and its proviso apply only to employees not covered by the first paragraph, i.e., casual employees (*Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.*, citing *Mercado*).

The correct basis is the general rule in the first paragraph. That paragraph excepts only seasonal work "for the duration of the season," i.e., one season. A seasonal employee employed for more than one season therefore falls under the general rule of regular employment. Regular seasonal employees are called to work from time to time, mostly during a season, and are temporarily laid off in the off-season. During the off-season they are not separated from service but are considered on leave until reemployed (*Abasolo*; *Gapayao*). Repeated hiring for the same tasks over several seasons is a badge of regular employment (*Universal Robina Sugar Milling Corp. v. Acibo*). From these cases the Court deduced two requisites: (1) the work or services are seasonal in nature; and (2) the employee is employed to perform them for more than one season. Both were present, and petitioners themselves admitted that Helen's seasonal work recurred every year.

**2. No, her freedom to work elsewhere is irrelevant.** Petitioners relied on *Mercado* as cited in *Gapayao*. *Hacienda Fatima* explained why *Mercado* does not apply here. In *Mercado*, the workers were hired "on and off for any single phase" of agricultural work, and the employer had the prerogative to take them in or not after each phase. Helen, by contrast, was hired repeatedly for the same activities: sugarcane cultivation, counting *patdan* (canepoints), and other sugar-farming work. Whether she was free to offer her services to others was therefore of no relevance. Her sari-sari store was likewise inconsequential and not incompatible with regular employment.

**3. No, pakyaw payment does not negate regular employment.** By raising this argument, petitioners were in effect asking the Court to re-examine the facts on whether an employer-employee relationship existed. That is not allowed in a Rule 45 review of a CA decision rendered under Rule 65. The inquiry is limited to whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC (*David v. Macasio*). Even if considered, the argument failed. A pakyaw or task basis arrangement "defines not the relationship between the parties but the manner of payment of wages" (*Abuda*). Pakyaw workers are regular employees if subject to the employer's control, and the control test "merely calls for the existence of the right to control, and not necessarily the exercise thereof" (*Gapayao*). Since Helen worked on petitioners' hacienda, they "could easily exercise control and supervision" over her, and whether they actually did so was immaterial. (This last inference was rejected in the August 11, 2025 Resolution.)
disposition:
The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The Court AFFIRMED the CA's Amended Decision dated January 9, 2015 and its Resolution dated July 20, 2015 in CA-G.R. SP No. 07025. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson), Hernando, Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. concurred.

The Court later SET ASIDE this Decision in its Resolution of August 11, 2025, which GRANTED the petition and REVERSED the CA.

bar_questions.q: Since 2015, Hacienda Esperanza, a sugarcane plantation, has hired Rosa every milling season to plant canepoints and weed the fields. She is laid off in the off-season and recalled at the start of the next season. It is undisputed that the hacienda's overseer prescribes how and when she does her tasks. In 2024 the hacienda stopped recalling her, saying that as a seasonal worker she was never a regular employee. In her illegal dismissal case, the Court of Appeals held Rosa a regular employee. It reasoned that she was a casual employee who became regular under the proviso of the second paragraph of Article 295 of the Labor Code, having rendered at least one year of service. (a) Is Rosa a regular employee? (b) Is the CA's reasoning correct?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, Rosa is a regular seasonal employee. (b) No. Her regular status rests on the first paragraph of Article 295, not on the proviso of the second paragraph.
alac.legal_basis: Under the first paragraph of Art. 295 (formerly Art. 280) of the Labor Code, the seasonal exception covers only employment "for the duration of the season." A seasonal employee becomes regular when (1) the employee performs work or services that are seasonal in nature and (2) is employed to perform such work for more than one season. The proviso of the second paragraph (one year of service, continuous or broken) applies only to casual employees, i.e., those not covered by the first paragraph. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023, citing Paz v. Northern Tobacco Redrying Co.)
alac.application: (a) Rosa's planting and weeding work is seasonal, and the hacienda has hired her for the same tasks every season since 2015, which is more than one season. Both requisites are met. An employer-employee relationship is undisputed, since the overseer controls how she works. Rosa is therefore a regular seasonal employee who is merely on leave during the off-season, and the hacienda's failure to recall her is a dismissal. (b) Rosa is a seasonal employee covered by the first paragraph of Art. 295, so she is not a casual employee. The second-paragraph proviso does not apply to her. Her regular status comes from the general rule in the first paragraph, because her employment is no longer for the duration of a single season.
alac.conclusion: Rosa is a regular seasonal employee, but under the first paragraph of Article 295, not the casual-employee proviso the CA used.

bar_questions.q: On a rice farm, the owner's foreman directs how all hired workers do their tasks. Ben has been hired every planting season for eight years to do the same work of plowing and transplanting. In the off-season he works on other farms and runs a small store. Carlo was hired for one harvest in 2023. Since then he has been taken in only on and off, for single phases of farm work, whenever the owner chooses to call him. The owner claims that neither is a regular employee because both are free to offer their services to other farm owners. Is the owner correct?

alac.answer: The owner is wrong as to Ben, who is a regular seasonal employee, but correct as to Carlo, who is not.
alac.legal_basis: A seasonal employee is regular if the employee performs seasonal work and is employed for it for more than one season. Freedom to offer one's services to others does not negate regular status, as long as the worker is hired repeatedly for the same activities and not merely on and off for any single phase of agricultural work. Mercado v. NLRC, where workers were not regular, involved workers hired "on and off for any single phase" of agricultural work, whom the employer could take in or not after each phase (Hacienda Fatima). (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023.)
alac.application: Ben is hired every season for the same tasks of plowing and transplanting, so his work is seasonal and his employment spans more than one season. His off-season work on other farms and his store do not matter, just as Helen's sari-sari store did not matter. Carlo's case is like Mercado. He is not rehired regularly and repeatedly for the same phase of work. He is called on and off for any single phase, at the owner's option. He therefore stays within the seasonal exception, and his freedom to work for others is simply the result of that on-and-off hiring.
alac.conclusion: Ben is a regular seasonal employee, while Carlo, hired only on and off for single phases, is not.

bar_questions.q: Hacienda Luz pays Dina on a pakyaw basis per hectare weeded. The hacienda's written work rules prescribe the tools, the method, and the order of weeding. They also authorize the overseer to stop and correct any worker. In practice, the overseer seldom visits Dina's plots. (a) The hacienda argues that the pakyaw arrangement and the lack of actual supervision negate any employer-employee relationship. Is it correct? (b) The NLRC found that Dina was a regular employee, and the CA affirmed on certiorari. The hacienda then files a Rule 45 petition asking the Supreme Court to re-weigh the evidence on control. What is the scope of the Court's review?

alac.answer: (a) No. Pakyaw is only a method of paying wages, and the control test requires only the right to control, which the hacienda has. (b) The Court reviews only whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC. It does not re-weigh the evidence, except in recognized exceptional cases.
alac.legal_basis: A pakyaw or task basis arrangement "defines not the relationship between the parties but the manner of payment of wages." Pakyaw workers are regular employees if subject to the employer's control, and the control test "merely calls for the existence of the right to control, and not necessarily the exercise thereof." In a Rule 45 review of a CA decision rendered under Rule 65 in a labor case, the narrow inquiry is whether the CA correctly determined the presence or absence of grave abuse of discretion by the NLRC. (Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel, G.R. No. 220087, November 13, 2023.) In the August 11, 2025 Resolution in the same case, the Court added two points. The right to control must cover the manner and means of the work and must be proven by substantial evidence. And the Court may review facts in exceptional cases, such as findings based on speculation or a misapprehension of facts.
alac.application: (a) Paying Dina per hectare only fixes how her wages are computed. The written rules give the hacienda the right to dictate the tools, method and sequence of her work, and to correct her, which is control over the manner and means. That right exists whether or not the overseer actually uses it, so the infrequent visits are immaterial. (b) The hacienda's petition raises a question of fact. The Court will ask only whether the CA correctly found no grave abuse of discretion in the NLRC's ruling. Since documentary evidence supports the finding of control, none of the exceptions that would justify a factual review applies.
alac.conclusion: Dina's pakyaw pay and the lack of actual supervision do not defeat her employment status, and the Court will not re-weigh the evidence under Rule 45.

notes: SET ASIDE ON RECONSIDERATION. See Hacienda San Isidro/Silos Farms v. Villaruel (Resolution), G.R. No. 220087, August 11, 2025 (case id gr-220087-20250811). That Resolution maintained this Decision's doctrine on the two requisites for regular seasonal employment and on pakyaw workers. It found, however, no substantial evidence that petitioners had the right to control the manner and means of Helen's work. It also said that Gapayao misappreciated Mercado and incompletely applied the control test. It granted the petition and reversed the CA, so Helen was ultimately not held a regular employee. This Decision's statement that petitioners "could easily exercise control" because Helen worked on their hacienda is no longer reliable, and the bar questions above therefore assume an established right of control. The Court's earlier minute resolutions (November 9, 2015 denying the petition; November 7, 2016 reinstating it) are known only from this Decision's recital. Lucito's case was not before the Court. The petition assailed the CA only as to Helen.

superseded_by.label: Set aside
superseded_by.summary: Set aside on reconsideration by the Resolution of August 11, 2025. The two requisites for regular seasonal employment were kept, but the worker must still prove the employer's right of control by substantial evidence, and the result was reversed.
